full_judgment:
1. Agrani Bank obtained a preliminary decree against writ petitioner Anwarul Bashir Khan and others in Writ Petition No. 5539 of 2005 on 7th May, 2001 in a suit for foreclosure being Mortgage Suit No. 49 of 1997. The decree was made final on 2nd August, 2001 for a sum of Taka 24,97,31,573. In pursuance thereof, the decree holder bank put the decree into execution in Title Execution Case No. 74 of 2001. In the said execution case Anwarul Bashir Khan filed an application under Order XXI, rule 83 of the Code of Civil Procedure for issuing a sale certificate in his favour in order to enable him to repay the decretal amount by selling one of the mortgaged properties situated at Gulshan. The Artha Rin Adalat rejected the prayer by order dated 14th November, 2002. Thereupon he challenged the said order in the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 6891 of 2002. The High Court Division summarily dismissed the writ petition by judgment and order dated 24th November, 2002 with a direction to the executing Court to "allow the petitioner to sell his Gulshan property first by granting necessary certificate to that effect within 3(three) months from the date of granting such certificate and for that the Court shall not be required to return the mortgage deed and/or the title documents to the petitioner before such sale." 

 2. Pursuant thereto the executing court issued a sale certificate on 4th April, 2004 enabling the judgment debtor to make the proposed sale of the mortgaged property. It was claimed that the judgment debtor entered into an agreement with Ragib Ali, the respondent No. 1 in Civil Appeal No. 106 of 2006, for transfer of the said mortgaged property at a consideration of Taka 1,95,00,000 on 16 June. 2004 and a sale deed was also executed on 7th July, 2004. Ragib Ali in turn prayed in the executing Court for confirmation of the sale and to accept the value. In the meantime one Kutub Uddin, the appellant in Civil Appeal No. 108 of 2008, filed an application expressing his eagerness to purchase the mortgaged property at Taka 4,00,46,250. The executing Court rejected the Ragib Ali's application and accepted the offer of Kutub Uddin. Kutub Uddin thereupon obtained a deed and prayed for delivery of possession. At this stage the judgment debtor moved Writ Petition No. 5539 of 2004 and Ragib Ali also moved Writ Petition No. 5590 of 2004 against that order. The High Court Division heard both the writ petitions analogously and made the rules absolute without, however, making any direction and/or making any declaration in terms of the rules. The decree-holder Agrani Bank and Kutub Uddin Ahmed thereupon sought leave from the judgment of the High Court Division. The leave was granted to consider whether the High Court Division was justified in making the rule absolute relying upon the judgment passed in earlier Writ Petition No. 6891 of 2002 which was apparently made in contravention of Order XXI, rule 83 (3) of the Code of Civil Procedure and also in violation of the principle of natural justice, inasmuch as, the direction was made without affording the Agrani Bank any opportunity of being heard. 

 5. When the judgment-debtor prayed for issuance of the sale certificate, the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 was in force under the said Ain, the Artha Rin Adalat was empowered to exercise all powers given to a Civil Court under the Code of Civil Procedure. Naturally, the provisions of the Code were applicable to a proceeding of the Artha Rin Adalat so far as they were not inconsistent with the Ain. There was no provision under the repealed Ain to issue any sale certificate of the mortgaged property in favour of a judgment-debtor. Order XXI, rule 83(1) provided for postponement of the sale for enabling the judgment-debtor to raise money for payment of the total amount by way of mortgage or lease or private sale of the property with the permission of the Court. The expression, the amount of the decree may be raised used in sub-rule (1) means the total decretal amount and not an amount which could not satisfy the decree, and no Court can grant such permission unless the entire debt can be realized by private alienation. This provision should be read subject to the provision of sub-rule (3) which is a non-obstante clause, which provides "Nothing in this rule shall be deemed to apply to a sale of property directed to be sold in execution of decree for sale in enforcement of a mortgage of, or charge on, such property". 

 6. So, sub-rule (1) does not apply to cases in which property is directed to be sold in execution of a decree on a mortgage. This is because, the decree holder or the creditor's right of sale, rests on the decree. If the judgment-debtor effected the alienation with the consent of the decree-holder, the implication of such sale would be otherwise. This is because by giving consent to the private sale the decree-holder does not become a holder of the decree for payment of money which is an essential condition for the applicability of section 73 of the Code. Therefore, there is no doubt that in case of a decree for foreclosure, be it the High Court Division, or any other superior Court, it has no power to issue certificate to alienate the mortgaged property for enabling the judgment-debtor to raise money for payment of the total decretal amount by private sale without the consent of the decree holder. The High Court Division had totally overlooked this bar and erroneously directed for the issuance of sale certificate in favour of the judgment-debtor. The direction was also exercised without affording the decree-holder bank an opportunity to defend the order and therefore, this order had no sanctity of law and the decree holder —as not bound by the said direction. Similarly, no right, title and interest in respect of the mortgaged property was conferred upon the purchaser Ragib Ali on the strength of the deed which was allegedly executed by the judgment debtor on the strength of an illegal sale certificate; it was issued in total violation of law. 

 7. True, the executing Court issued a sale-certificate in favour of the judgment-debtor but that was made on the basis of the direction given by the superior court which direction was made ignoring the provisions of law applicable to the case. Under such circumstances, the executing Court had no other alternative but to follow the said direction. Since the direction was made violating the provisions of law, it had no force of law. Therefore, we find force in the contention made on behalf of the decree-holder bank that the direction being per-incursion, it was not binding upon the decree-holder as well as the executing Court. This transaction of sale was made collusively, which is apparent from the fact that it was sold at Taka 1,95,00,000 against the total decretal amount of Taka 24,97,31,573. Even if it is assumed that only one property was sold leaving aside the other two properties, in view of sale of the same property at Taka 4,00,46,250 during the relevant time it is apparent that the market value of the property was much higher than the amount shown in the deed.
